title: Creativity and Inspiration: Beating Writer's Block
description: A course for anyone who wants to write, or make anything, and keeps getting stuck. It starts with what psychologists have found about creativity: how ideas form, why they often arrive after a break, and why limits can help more than they hurt. It then explains why blocks happen, using Mike Rose's studies of blocked student writers and Robert Boice's studies of blocked professors, and turns that evidence into methods you can use tomorrow. Every chapter ends with a writing exercise, so you finish with a habit and a stack of pages, not just ideas.
prerequisites: None; a notebook or a document you can write in is enough
A writing project you care about, large or small (helpful but not required)
objectives: Explain divergent and convergent thinking and point to each in your own writing process.
Describe Wallas's four stages of creative work and summarize what experiments show about incubation.
Diagnose a writing block using Rose's analysis of rigid rules and plans and Boice's findings on bingeing and perfectionism.
Set up a scheduled writing routine and keep a log of minutes and words for at least four weeks.
Use freewriting, idea capture and chosen constraints to produce material on demand.
Revise a draft in separate passes for structure, paragraphs and sentences.
Tell research findings apart from practitioner advice and judge how strong each claim about inspiration is.

preface:
This book is for anyone who wants to write and keeps not writing. Maybe you stare at a blank page, or start strong and stall halfway, or wait for a mood that rarely comes. You are in good company, and here is the good news: being stuck has been studied. Researchers have watched blocked writers at work, counted their pages, and tested what helps.

We begin with what creativity research says: how ideas form, why the answer often turns up after you walk away, and why a limit can help you more than a blank page. Then we look at why blocks happen, through two careful studies of stuck writers: Mike Rose's work with college students and Robert Boice's work with professors. The second half turns that evidence into methods: writing on a schedule, freewriting, catching ideas, choosing constraints and revising in passes.

Pick one project in Chapter 1, anything you want to write, and bring it to every chapter. Each chapter ends with a timed writing exercise, and you will keep a small log of what you wrote. When an idea comes from research, I will tell you how strong the evidence is; when it comes from a writer's experience, I will say that too. By the end you will have a routine, a log that shows it working, and pages you did not have before.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a writing researcher who also writes every day: claims about creativity come from psychology and composition research (Sawyer and Henriksen, Rose, Boice, Silvia), practitioner advice is labeled as practitioner advice, and every idea is tried on the page in the same chapter.
bible.promise: By the last page you will know why you get stuck, have a writing routine that does not wait for inspiration, and have finished pages to show for it.
threads: Generate first, judge later: divergent and convergent thinking are different jobs.
Habits beat moods: regular scheduled writing is the best-supported answer to blocking.
Blocks have causes you can find (rigid rules, perfectionism, binge writing), so they can be fixed.
Research or practitioner wisdom: say which is which, and how strong the evidence is.
Write in every chapter: each one ends with pages, not just notes.

runningExamples.name: Your project
runningExamples.use: One piece of writing the reader chooses in Chapter 1 (a story, essay, blog post, song, or the store description and devlog for a game) and works on in every exercise. Readers of Video Game Marketing (GMK 201) can use their game's store page text.

runningExamples.name: Rose's blocked and unblocked students
runningExamples.use: Case studies from Writer's Block: The Cognitive Dimension (1984), used in Chapters 5 and 7 to contrast rigid rules with flexible ones.

runningExamples.name: Boice's scheduled-writing study
runningExamples.use: His 1983 comparison of writers who abstained, wrote when they felt like it, or wrote on a schedule with consequences; introduced in Chapter 5 and central to Chapter 6, with its small sample stated.

runningExamples.name: The writing log
runningExamples.use: A simple record of minutes, words and new ideas per session that the reader starts in Chapter 1 and uses as evidence about their own habits.

conventions: Label every claim's source: a study (with year and who was studied), a review, or practitioner advice.
Say plainly when a finding comes from a small, old or lab-only study.
Use 'block' in Rose's sense: an inability to begin or continue writing for reasons other than a lack of skill or commitment.
Every chapter ends with a writing exercise timed in minutes, with a word or page count the reader logs.
Give a person's full name at first mention in a chapter, with the year of the work cited.

canon.cite: Sawyer, R. K., & Henriksen, D. (2024). Explaining creativity: The science of human innovation (3rd ed.). Oxford University Press.
canon.role: Main research textbook: definitions of creativity, divergent and convergent thinking, Wallas's stages, incubation and insight, and creativity under constraints.

canon.cite: Rose, M. (1984). Writer's block: The cognitive dimension. Southern Illinois University Press.
canon.role: Primary study of blocking in college writers: rigid rules and conflicting plans versus flexible ones; Chapters 5 and 7. Reissued in 2009 with a new preface.

canon.cite: Boice, R. (1990). Professors as writers: A self-help guide to productive writing. New Forums Press.
canon.role: Research-based program from Boice's studies of blocked academic writers: spontaneous and generative writing, brief scheduled sessions, and handling relapse; Chapters 5 and 6.

canon.cite: Silvia, P. J. (2019). How to write a lot: A practical guide to productive academic writing (2nd ed.). American Psychological Association.
canon.role: Practical scheduled-writing method from a creativity researcher: fixed times, goals and tracking; Chapter 6. An advice book grounded in research, not itself a study.

canon.cite: Csikszentmihalyi, M. (1996). Creativity: Flow and the psychology of discovery and invention. HarperCollins.
canon.role: Interviews with nearly one hundred highly creative people, the systems view (person, domain, field) and flow; Chapters 1 and 3. Interviews show how creators describe their work, not what causes creativity.

canon.cite: Lamott, A. (1994). Bird by bird: Some instructions on writing and life. Pantheon Books.
canon.role: Practitioner book, not research: short assignments, rough first drafts and quieting the inner critic; quoted for craft advice in Chapters 7 and 8 and labeled as one writer's experience.

bible.care: Present creativity research at its real strength: many findings come from lab tasks, small samples or interviews, and the book says so. Keep practitioner advice (Lamott, the tips in Silvia and Boice) labeled as such. Do not promise that any method cures every block. Chapter 5 says plainly that long-lasting inability to write together with low mood, loss of interest or anxiety that affects daily life can be depression or an anxiety disorder, and that a doctor or counselor can help. Do not repeat popular myths as fact (left-brain and right-brain creativity, the tortured genius, creativity as a fixed gift).
